title: The Kindertransport
hookLine: Jewish children are sent to Britain by train and ship, without their parents

cards: A railway platform, crowded and strangely quiet. A small girl wears her good coat. Around her neck hangs a cardboard tag with a number on it.
She holds one small suitcase, packed by her mother the night before: a few clothes, a photograph, maybe a book. Her parents are kissing her goodbye. They are not getting on the train.
Only she is. The whistle blows. Today's word is the name of that train, and of all the trains like it.

teach.b: Kindertransport is German for children's transport. After Kristallnacht, Britain agreed to take in Jewish children from Germany, Austria and nearby lands. Not their parents.
Just the children. Jewish groups, Quakers and other volunteers raced to arrange it: lists, papers, families or hostels on the other side, people willing to promise each child's keep.

teach.h: TRAIN, SHIP, A HOME OF STRANGERS.
teach.b: The children went by train to the coast, then by ship across the sea, and were met by strangers. Some were taken into loving homes. Some were moved from place to place.

Some were the only Jewish child in a village. When the war began, the way out all but closed, and the rescue nearly ended. For some of the children, that platform was the last time they saw their parents.
The Torah tells of a mother who does the same impossible thing. In Egypt, Pharaoh orders the Hebrew baby boys killed.
Moses' mother hides him as long as she can, then makes a little ark of reeds, lays him in it, and sets it among the reeds at the river's edge. She lets go of her child to save him.
And the Torah adds one line about his older sister: "And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him." Someone watched. Someone wanted to know where he went.
Today's word holds two things at once, and neither cancels the other.
It was a rescue: children lived who might not have.
And it was a goodbye: every child on those trains was someone's whole world, handed to strangers by parents who stayed behind.

how: Survivors of the Kindertransport and their families have gathered and recorded their stories, and Jewish communities and schools remember the rescue alongside the parents who stayed behind.

games.q: you are a Jewish parent in Germany after Kristallnacht. there is a place on a train to Britain for your child, and no place for you. what did the parents of the Kindertransport children choose?
o: keep your child with you, whatever comes.
pack one small suitcase and let your child go alone.
wait until the whole family can leave together.
games.why: parents put their children on the trains and stayed behind. like Moses' mother at the river, they let go of their child to save them.

practice: Bring to mind one child on that platform, with a tag and a small suitcase, then the parents standing still as the train pulls out, and breathe with both of them.
If it's too heavy, let your attention rest on your own breath for a while, and come back when you're ready. If you pray, hold them in prayer; if you don't, just keep them company.

wordCard.voice: The Kindertransport. German for children's transport: the rescue that brought Jewish children to Britain, without their parents, in the months before the war. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the children went alone. A rescue and a goodbye, both at once. Be gentle with yourself.
